title: Matching Receipts
story: You went on a trip with a friend and paid for everything. Back home, your friend sends you money for exactly two of your receipts. The message only says the total: target.
You have a list of receipt amounts in the order you paid them. Which two receipts was your friend paying for?
task: Write findPair(amounts, target). Return the positions (indexes) of the two receipts whose amounts add up to target. You can return them in either order.
Each receipt can be used once. There is always exactly one correct pair.
constraints: Exactly one pair of different positions adds up to target.

examples.explanation: 25 + 75 = 100. Those receipts sit at positions 1 and 2. No other pair works: 40 would need a 60, and 15 would need an 85.
Two different receipts can have the same amount. 5 + 5 = 10, using position 0 and position 1. Using position 0 twice would not count.

hints: Pick any one receipt, say the 25 in the first example. If it is part of the answer, what must the other receipt's amount be?
For each receipt a, the partner must be exactly target - a. So the real question at every step is: have I already seen the amount target - a, and where?
Which data structure answers "have I seen this value, and at what position?" in one step, instead of scanning the whole list again?

Walk the list once, left to right. Keep a hash map from amount to position. At each receipt, look up target - a first. If it is in the map, you are done. If not, store a with its position and move on. Looking up before storing stops a receipt from pairing with itself.
bruteForce: Try every pair: for each position i, check every later position j and see if amounts[i] + amounts[j] === target.

It is correct, and a fine first step. But with 10,000 receipts that is about 50 million pairs, because the number of pairs grows with n². The slow part is the inner loop: it searches the whole list for a partner every time.

walkthrough: The brute force searches for a partner from scratch for every receipt. The fix is to remember what you have already passed, so finding a partner is one lookup.
• Position 0, amount 40. Need 60. The map is empty, so no. Store 40 → 0.
• Position 1, amount 25. Need 75. Not in the map. Store 25 → 1.
• Position 2, amount 75. Need 25. The map has 25 → 1. Return [1, 2].
Notice the order inside the loop: look up first, then store. If you stored first, a receipt of 50 with target 100 would find itself.
solution.timeWhy: One pass over the list, and each hash map lookup or insert is O(1) on average.
solution.spaceWhy: In the worst case the map holds every amount before the pair is found.
solution.takeaway: When you need to find a partner for each element, store what you have seen in a hash map and ask for the partner directly. This trades O(n) memory for dropping an entire loop.
